talks.title: Watch The Streamathon today Dec 18
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cybersecurity Cares - Watch The Streamathon today Dec 18.
talks.summary:
Overview: Nicole from the Diana Initiative promotes the Cyber Security Cares Streamathon fundraiser supporting nonprofits that make cybersecurity healthier, more inclusive, and more sustainable.

Key Topics: Diversity barriers in information security; Diana Initiative programs including RSA and DEF CON scholar sponsorships; quiet rooms and community spaces at DEF CON; and the December fundraising campaign splitting proceeds among five nonprofits.

Technical Details: The Initiative sponsored scholars to RSA, Black Hat, and DEF CON with mentorship programs, hosted neurodivergent-friendly spaces, and supported BSides events in New York, Delaware, and Philadelphia during the prior year.

Takeaways: Cybersecurity's diversity problem requires sustained community investment. Supporting organizations like the Diana Initiative builds a healthier, more representative security workforce.

talks.title: OWASP
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b analyzes OWASP.
talks.summary:
OWASP at Hacker Summer Camp

In a Hacker Summer Camp 101 interview, OWASP representative John explains the group’s Def Con outreach showing hackers and white hats share a skill spectrum. OWASP hosts hands-on trainings rather than lecture-only sessions for newcomers and veterans alike.

Hands-On Villages and Workshops

Planned activities include Juice Shop training, Hadex sessions, and ZAP plugin labs. OWASP also runs an intentionally vulnerable AI boot camp for participants who have never tried breaking ML systems. A lounge offers one-on-one help, including support for visitors in partner villages such as Blue Team Village CTFs.

Community Cross-Village Alignment

John recommends bringing a laptop for interactive workshops but warns against daily-driver devices—referencing Def Con “YOLO” burners. OWASP coordinates with Adversarial Village, Red Team Village, IC, Lonely Hackers, Diana, and WISP for cross-village learning experiences.

talks.title: Lonely Hackers Club
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b details Lonely Hackers Club.
talks.summary:
Community Purpose

Star from Lonely Hackers Club (LHC) clarifies the group is not a dating site—it is a welcoming DEF CON crew for solo travelers who want friends before arriving. Originating from r/DEFCON repeat questions about hotels, parties, and badges, LHC keeps thousands registered with ~1,000 active on Telegram year-round.

Onboarding and Safety

Newcomers join via lonelyhackers.com/club Telegram, find mentors before con, and avoid first-timer panic (e.g., locating goons for badges). Host Nicole from The Diana Initiative recommends Hacker Summer Camp 101 resources, Hacker Tracker, and info booth or red-shirt goons when lost.

DEF CON Activities

LHC collaborates with OWASP, TDI, and others on resume reviews, CTFs, badge builds, workshops, and social events like group dinners (including social-engineering steakhouse outings). They occupy community space near TDI with content throughout the con, not a brief pop-up village.

Audience and Merch

Kids are generally discouraged except mature teen volunteers. LHC prioritizes community over sales, though electronic badges may appear; Telegram remains the primary engagement channel.

talks.title: Pinball High Score Contest
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b examines Pinball High Score Contest.
talks.summary:
Pinball at DEF CON

Rich, a world-ranked competitive pinball player, describes how pinball became a DEF CON fixture. After years of visiting the Pinball Hall of Fame, he researched IoT-era pinball machines, found vulnerabilities that could remotely flip flippers during high-stakes tournaments, and disclosed them at ShmooCon. Stern Pinball then partnered to bring machines on-site so attendees would not have to leave the conference.

Pinball High Score Contest

Last year's contest was deliberately layered: hints appeared in forums, social media, and GitHub, and game code/settings were arranged so careful observers could hack into the finals without breaking equipment or the network. A village worker won after reporting an unfair game configuration. The event also tied into Stern Insider Connected QR badges, privacy guidance, IFPA-sanctioned play, and cross-village CTF flags embedded in games.

Advice for participants

Rich encourages newcomers to walk up and play, try unconventional paths, and ask volunteers when unsure. DEF CON contests often reward creative rule interpretation within stated boundaries.

talks.title: XR Village
talks.teaser: HSC101 Hacker Summer Camp n00b analyzes XR Village.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Diana Initiative's Hacker Summer Camp 101 episode introduces DEF CON's XR Village with organizer Star, covering extended-reality security and community activities.

## What XR Village Covers
"Extended reality" spans AR, VR, MR, and even persona-driven gameplay that alters perceived reality. The village hosts hardware hacking on VR headsets, social-engineering exercises, and kid-friendly challenges.

## Community Highlights
A favorite activity pairs kids with federal demo-lab operators—coaching youngsters to socially engineer serious-looking government techs into silly tasks. A 14-year-old partnered with Meta became the village's top VR hardware hacker, returning annually.

## Takeaways
XR Village blends physical device security, human manipulation skills, and inclusive outreach—visit for stickers, badge swaps, and hands-on XR threat exploration.

talks.title: Redefining Strength: The Power of Leading
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Redefining Strength: The Power of Leading with Empathy and Embracing Vulnerability.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, cybersecurity executive and CEO Rick discusses redefining leadership strength through empathy, vulnerability, and inclusivity. Drawing on twenty years of experience in go-to-market roles across security companies such as Rapid7, Bugcrowd, Sonatype, and currently KSOC, Rick contrasts traditional command-and-control, extrovert-centric leadership styles with empathetic, human-centered approaches that foster psychological safety and team success.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Leadership Styles**: The shift from traditional models where vulnerability was viewed as weakness and extroversion was prioritized, toward models that accommodate diverse personalities and backgrounds.
- **Challenges Faced by Female Leaders**: Common biases and double standards in cybersecurity, including doubts about technical expertise, questions regarding co-founders, and pressure to adopt aggressive leadership demeanors.
- **The Business Case for Diversity**: Research demonstrating positive business outcomes associated with female leadership, such as stock price momentum, improved profitability, and greater gender diversity on boards.
- **Empathy in the Workplace and Culture**: Adopting core values—such as those used at Microsoft—that evaluate individuals not only on personal business impact but also on how they contribute to the success of others.
- **Supportive Company Policies**: Practical mechanisms to support employees, including generous parental leave policies for both mothers and fathers, mental health breaks, and meeting-free Fridays.

### Technical Details & Actionable Practices
Rick highlights five foundational behaviors to cultivate empathy and minimize workplace conflict:
1. **Be Present**: Disconnect from digital distractions and remain engaged during interactions.
2. **Active Listening**: Restate or summarize what others communicate to validate their perspectives and ensure they feel heard.
3. **Invest in Self-Care**: Leaders must recharge physically and mentally (e.g., exercise, taking breaks) to maintain the capacity to support others effectively.
4. **Assume Positive Intent**: Prevent workplace friction by operating under the baseline assumption that colleagues are acting in good faith rather than with malicious motives.
5. **Follow Up**: Check in regularly after discussions or difficult moments to reinforce long-term care and accountability.

### Q&A Insights and Takeaways
During the audience question-and-answer period, several leadership challenges were addressed:
- **Integrating Empathy into Onboarding**: Embedding culture into new hire orientation across departments so core values are introduced immediately.
- **Balancing Empathy with Business Performance**: Acknowledging that while leaders should not act as full-time therapists, empathetic evaluation metrics naturally curb toxic behaviors by aligning personal success with team support.
- **Scaling Company Culture and HR**: Managing HR's role as organizations expand, ensuring employee support remains genuine rather than strictly bureaucratic.
- **Setting Boundaries**: Demonstrating and respecting transparent schedule boundaries (e.g., blocking personal time, disconnecting Slack after hours) tailored to individual team needs rather than enforcing a rigid one-size-fits-all model.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Diana Initiative 2022, Ayan Islam—Associate Policy Director of Cybersecurity and Emerging Threats at the R Street Institute and former IT specialist at CISA—addresses the significant divide between frontline cybersecurity practitioners and policymakers. Islam argues that while there is an enormous workforce deficit in cybersecurity broadly, an even sharper deficit exists in legislative and policy bodies. Practitioners with operational, hands-on experience are desperately needed to inform policymaking to ensure laws, regulations, and executive actions are technically sound and operationally feasible.

### Key Topics
- **Legislative Knowledge Deficit:** As of 2015, only seven out of 3,500 legislative staff had formal technology training. While programs like Tech Congress helped raise this number above 65, Congress faces an influx of proposed legislation—over 498 cybersecurity-related proposals in the current session alone, with nine passing into law.
- **Operational Consequences of Policy:** Disconnects frequently arise between high-level policy mandates and frontline implementation. As an example, the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) of 2021 mandates ransomware incident and data breach reporting for critical infrastructure entities to CISA within specific timeframes. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) face practical hurdles aggregating, triaging, and automating logs to meet these compliance demands without breaking ongoing operations.
- **Pathways for Engagement:** Practitioners can bridge the silo through several structured avenues:
  - *Fellowships:* Programs such as Tech Congress, CISA’s Innovation Fellows program, and the Google Public Policy Fellowship.
  - *Community & Advocacy Initiatives:* Efforts like Share the Mic in Cyber to elevate underrepresented practitioners, particularly Black cybersecurity professionals.
  - *Grassroots & Industry Groups:* I Am The Cavalry, sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs) such as Aviation ISAC and Financial Services ISAC, and localized efforts like the Michigan Cyber Civilian Corps or local BSides events.
  - *Public Writing and Commenting:* Submitting public comments on proposed rules, publishing blog posts, and authoring op-eds.

### Technical Details & Implementation Context
Islam highlights that policy decisions directly dictate technical priorities. For instance, incident reporting rules require organizations to build automated logging pipelines and incident response triage workflows capable of producing regulatory disclosures rapidly. When technical practitioners participate early—such as redlining draft bills, participating in ISAC working groups, or commenting during agency rulemaking—they help prevent regulations that create unintended operational disruption in areas like Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and SCADA environments.

### Takeaways
- Cyber practitioners must view their operational experience as valuable input for public policy.
- Companies should consider investing in in-house cyber policy teams that actively collaborate with software developers, engineers, and subject matter experts.
- Engaging directly—via fellowship leaves of absence, industry working groups, grassroots bodies, or formal public comments—ensures that technical realities shape future cyber legislation.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Charu Bansal-Navigating the Imposter Syndrome
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Diana Initiative 2021-Charu Bansal-Navigating the Imposter Syndrome.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk at the Diana Initiative 2021, Charu Bansal shares her personal journey and practical strategies for navigating imposter syndrome within the cybersecurity industry. Transitioning from a liberal arts background with no formal technical education to serving as an Information Systems Security Officer (ISSO) for a global enterprise, Bansal addresses the pervasive feeling of inadequacy often experienced in technical environments. She highlights why the condition cannot simply be permanently cured, framing it instead as an ongoing navigation process, and provides actionable advice for both individuals facing imposter syndrome and mentors supporting them.

### Key Topics
- **Personal Background and Transition:** Growing up in rural Himalayas with limited access to technology, Bansal pivoted from liberal arts into security seven years prior when a team took a chance on her. Her early days involved learning foundational terms like penetration testing, man-in-the-middle, and Burp Suite while navigating underrepresentation as one of few women at technical conferences.
- **Knowledge vs. Intelligence:** Bansal emphasizes that not knowing specific jargon, tools, or acronyms does not indicate a lack of intelligence. Intelligence is the capacity to learn, and technical knowledge can be acquired through self-directed study, security podcasts, newsletters, community meetups, and conferences.
- **Rejecting Limiting Boxes:** She cautions against allowing colleagues to pigeonhole individuals into non-technical administrative tasks (e.g., solely taking meeting notes or maintaining Confluence pages) under the assumption that they cannot handle technical or engineering discussions.
- **Non-Technical Strengths in Security:** Security is inherently rooted in human behavior, not merely technical problems. Bansal discusses how non-traditional backgrounds provide critical perspectives in threat modeling, cross-border payment platforms, incident response planning, and creative phishing exercises through an understanding of international laws, cultural differences, and life experiences.
- **Mentorship and Support:** Effective mentoring requires genuine dialogue to understand a mentee's exact knowledge gaps rather than overwhelming them with generic resources (such as lengthy course lists or extensive GitHub links) or doing the work for them.

### Technical Details
- **Threat Modeling Integration:** Threat modeling is highlighted as a collaborative exercise aimed at identifying and proactively mitigating potential threats to systems, processes, or applications. Bansal illustrates how life experiences—such as anticipating what could go wrong when moving across continents—translate directly into threat modeling frameworks, including evaluating payment methods and threat vectors on a global payment platform.
- **Human Factors in Incident Planning:** Non-technical domain expertise, including familiarity with multi-jurisdictional legal and regulatory requirements, contributes directly to incident response planning, while behavioral insights inform anti-phishing simulations.

### Takeaways
- **Normalize Asking for Help:** Imposter syndrome thrives when individuals hide their struggles out of fear of exposure. The security community must normalize admitting knowledge gaps and asking for guidance.
- **Show Up Prepared:** When faced with intimidating meetings, demand an agenda, research unfamiliar terms beforehand, and continuously show up and listen attentively even if only a fraction of the discussion is immediately understood.
- **Guidance for Mentors:** Mentors should prioritize targeted teaching over fixing issues for mentees, avoiding resource overload and establishing mutual trust through targeted questions.
- **Internal Affirmation:** Acknowledge your accomplishments and bravery in challenging established industry biases, reframing self-doubt with the reminder that diverse perspectives provide vital security value.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Diana Initiative 2021-Duane Dunston-Mentoring and Training Experts: A cognitive science approach.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Dwayne Dunston, an associate professor of cyber security at Champlain College with 24+ years of industry experience, presents a cognitive science approach to mentoring and training cybersecurity experts. This talk is a follow-up to his previous Diana Initiative presentation, addressing concerns about scalability raised by an audience member.

## Key Concepts
Dunston distinguishes between novices (those new to a domain who rely on critical thinking, problem-solving, and mimicking) and experts (those with domain-specific knowledge). He introduces the Expert Reversal Effect from cognitive load theory: methods effective for training novices can actually be detrimental to experts because they may undo long-term schemas already built up, especially in graded educational settings.

## Training Experts Through Deliberate Practice
Unlike novices who need structured instruction, experts need coaching and advice rather than feedback. Dunston defines deliberate practice as repetitive, willful attempts to improve performance—distinguishing it from general practice. He emphasizes that quality of experience matters far more than hours spent; 24 years of experience provides less expertise development than focused deliberate practice on specific weaknesses.

Key principles for expert development include:
- **Dynamic Practice**: Mentors must know their mentees well enough to adjust difficulty levels, progressively pushing them to apply skills in new contexts
- **Mentor-Mentee Relationship**: Regular check-ins and communication enable correction of mistakes and refinement of weak skills
- **Cognitive Apprenticeship**: The mentor makes thinking visible, provides feedback, allows reflection, and observes the mentee's work

## Practical Methods
Dunston illustrates his approach through his own experience learning Mitre ATT&CK Cyber Threat Intelligence. Rather than self-study, he engaged a mentor who provided threat intelligence reports for him to map against the framework, met regularly for guided feedback and advice, and progressively tackled harder scenarios across different domains (universities, industrial control systems).

For training providers, he recommends:
- **Case Studies**: Recreate real industry incidents from fire eye or Mandiant reports and have students solve them before reviewing the expert solution
- **Community-Driven Hard Problems**: Establish databases of hard problems across threat hunting, incident response, threat intelligence, and reverse engineering. Example: Honeynet Project's approach of posting attack PCAPs for community analysis and expert review
- **Worked Examples**: Show step-by-step how to perform tasks rather than directing learners to "google it"

## Takeaways
Mentoring experts requires understanding individual needs and capabilities. While some aspects of novice training apply to experts (particularly worked examples), the emphasis shifts to coaching, deliberate practice on specific weak areas, and progressive difficulty increases. A community database of hard problems could enable experts to pursue deliberate practice in their specific skill gaps, addressing the scalability concern from the previous year's talk.

talks.title: Diana Initiative 2021-Julie Carres-A N00bHacker's Guide to the Infosec Galaxy
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Diana Initiative 2021-Julie Carres-A N00bHacker's Guide to the Infosec Galaxy.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Diana Initiative 2021 session, speaker Julie Carres—a math teacher with an art history degree who transitioned into infosec via DEF CON and was accepted into the SANS Women's Immersion Academy—delivers a comprehensive guide for beginners ("noobs") looking to learn information security. Emphasizing that reading dense technical books late at night after work can be exhausting, Carres advocates for gamified, hands-on learning aligned with personal learning styles to keep self-study engaging and sustainable.

### Key Topics
- **Learning Archetypes (Alice vs. Jill):** Carres categorizes learners into two profiles based on how they explore topics:
  - *Alice (Deep Dive Specialist):* Tends to go down rabbit holes, demanding to understand underlying mechanics completely before moving on. Alices benefit from resources that push them to broaden their scope across multiple disciplines rather than getting stuck on a single challenge or topic.
  - *Jill (Broad Generalist):* Curious about everything, skims many topics, and is quick to experiment, but risks lacking deep foundational knowledge. Jills benefit from structured curriculums that force them to narrow their focus and follow paths through to completion.
- **Capture the Flag (CTF) Platforms:** CTFs provide structured, low-pressure, gamified learning environments that cater to both archetypes:
  - *TryHackMe:* Features guided learning paths (such as complete beginner tracks, web security, and offensive pentesting), succinct modular lessons, and in-browser VMs/attack boxes.
  - *PicoCTF:* Created by Carnegie Mellon, offering jeopardy-style challenges covering cryptography, binary exploitation, web exploitation, and more across varied difficulty levels with built-in web shells.
  - *OverTheWire:* War game site (notably the Bandit track) focused on practical Linux command-line skills, SSH, and search methodology using a repetitive, scaffolding pedagogical approach.
  - *SANS Holiday Hack Challenge:* An annually updated, MMO-style puzzle environment with avatars, narrative quests, and community write-ups available after winners are announced.
- **Learning to Code:** While not every infosec role requires development experience, familiarity with scripting, web technologies, or reverse engineering concepts is highly valuable. Recommended pathways range from academic courses (edX CS50, Coursera Princeton Java, Georgia Tech Python) to gamified interactive tools (Scratch block coding, CodeCombat RPG, and Codecademy).
- **Crypto Challenges & "Chall" Sites:** Static challenge resources like Rank.org, NewbieContest.org, NotPron, and US Cyber Command Valentine's Day crypto challenges provide puzzles that test mathematical reasoning, cryptography, and problem-solving without easily accessible answer keys.
- **Projects and Family Engagement:** Practical suggestions for applying skills and demonstrating aptitude without a formal tech resume include writing technical blog posts/write-ups, setting up home lab hypervisors with VulnHub machines, configuring a network-wide ad-blocking Pi-hole, and engaging family members through Scratch Jr, cryptographic scavenger hunts, or CyberStart America.

### Technical Details
- **CTF Fundamentals:** Digital security competitions revolving around locating hidden text strings ("flags"), typically enclosed in curly brackets and often written in leetspeak.
- **Linux CLI Mastery:** OverTheWire's Bandit builds essential terminal skills incrementally (connecting via `ssh`, exploring directories with `ls`, finding files, inspecting permissions) where the output of one level serves as the credential for the next.
- **Home Networking & DNS:** Running a Raspberry Pi-hole serves as a hands-on project to learn local DNS configuration, network traffic troubleshooting, and basic server management.

### Takeaways
- Align study resources with personal tendencies: "Alices" need structure to broaden their perspective, while "Jills" need curriculums to maintain depth and focus.
- Gamified platforms and write-up walkthroughs provide safe, accessible environments to reverse-engineer solutions when stuck.
- Developing a technical blog and documenting CTF write-ups or hands-on home projects acts as an effective portfolio for career transitions into infosec.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Diana Initiative 2020 - Abhijith B R (abx) - Internal Red Team Operations Framework - Building ....
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Diana Initiative 2020, Abhijith B R (known as abx) presents a structured methodology called the Internal Red Team Operations Framework (IRTOF). The framework is designed to help organizations transition from traditional internal penetration testing and vulnerability assessments toward a mature, practical internal red teaming program. The speaker emphasizes that while vulnerability assessments produce exhaustive lists of flaws and penetration tests focus on compromising specific targets, red teaming represents a full-scope adversarial simulation aimed at testing people, processes, and technology across the entire organization to systematically enhance defensive capabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Distinction Between Disciplines**: Clarifying the differences between vulnerability assessment (listing all potential weaknesses), penetration testing (goal-oriented compromise of specific targets), and red teaming (full-scope adversarial simulation aimed at challenging defensive measures).
- **The IRTOF Phased Progression**: A five-phase progressive roadmap modeled from "crawling" to "flying" (Phase 1: Crawling, Phase 2, Phase 3, Phase 4: Running, and Phase 5: Flying).
- **Team Composition and Skill Sets**: Building a multidisciplinary offensive unit inspired by diverse teams like The A-Team, including both deeply technical operators and non-technical advisors who can assist with realistic social engineering and business communications.
- **Collaboration with Blue Teams**: Emphasizing that red teams exist to make defenders stronger, advocating for continuous purple teaming and constructive relationships rather than adversarial friction.
- **Strategic vs. Tactical Execution**: Structuring the framework as individual short-term tactical plans (spanning 3 to 6 months per phase) chained together into an overarching long-term strategic plan.

### Technical Details
IRTOF breaks down red team maturity into five distinct phases:
1. **Phase 1 (Crawling / Foundation)**: Securing executive budget approval, establishing rules of engagement with legal and leadership oversight, defining clear objectives focused on protecting critical organizational crown jewels and sensitive data, identifying vulnerable key personnel, evaluating the existing security posture, and recruiting core talent.
2. **Phase 2 (Initial Operations & Emulation)**: Setting up external infrastructure (cloud environments, domain names, email hosting) and leveraging open-source command-and-control (C2) frameworks, implants, and tools. Initiating adversary emulation using open-source resources like MITRE ATT&CK, Atomic Red Team, and Caldera to test antivirus, EDR, and SOC logging. Mapping external attack surfaces, establishing remediation processes, and running basic phishing campaigns across employee tiers to test mail filters and proxy controls.
3. **Phase 3 (Improvisation & Process Maturation)**: Advancing tools, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) when standard methods are restricted (e.g., employing unmanaged PowerShell when standard PowerShell is blocked). Testing and attempting continuous EDR and antivirus bypasses, identifying exploitation paths toward crown jewels, evaluating incident response times and containment procedures, conducting automated emulation campaigns across random machines, and drafting formal operational documentation.
4. **Phase 4 (Running / Collaboration & Physical Assessment)**: Transitioning into continuous, collaborative purple team exercises and incorporating enterprise tooling alongside open-source platforms. Executing targeted spear-phishing campaigns against executives and management using custom tooling rather than easily detectable frameworks. Conducting overt physical security assessments (official walk-throughs inspecting doors, locks, RFID checkpoints, and CCTV, referencing work by Deviant Ollam) with proper operational security (avoiding tactical backpacks or sticker-covered laptops), and instituting continuous operator/defender training.
5. **Phase 5 (Flying / Full Maturity)**: Achieving advanced internal capabilities, including internally developed custom C2 platforms, custom implants, and exploit scripts. Running a formal purple team metrics model to evaluate blue team coverage and red team progress. Conducting covert physical security assessments once organizational trust and confidence are established, executing continuous adversary simulation, and running iterative cycles of the IRTOF operational process.

### Takeaways
Building an effective internal red team requires incremental growth rather than jumping immediately into complex, covert operations. By viewing each IRTOF phase as an achievable 3-to-6-month tactical plan, security leaders can progressively assemble diverse talent, establish open-source infrastructure, advance to custom development, and integrate collaborative purple team exercises that continually challenge and enhance the organization's overall cyber defense posture.
